outcome: Brayden Casella found a non-terminating game of Beggar-My-Neighbour on 10 February 2024 (a cyclical structure of 62 tricks reached by 30 distinct starting hands, looping after 474 turns/66 tricks), the construction and proof were written up with seven collaborators as an arXiv preprint on 19 March 2024, and the result was peer-reviewed and published in The American Mathematical Monthly (vol. 132, no. 10, pp. 978-994) on 20 October 2025, answering the question in the affirmative.

counterexample.object: A pair of starting hands (26 cards each) for Beggar-My-Neighbour that produce an eventually-periodic, non-terminating game: a cyclical structure of 62 tricks reached after some initial play from 30 distinct starting hands, with the concrete pair given as '---K---Q-KQAJ-----AAJ--J--' and '----------Q----KQ-J-----KA'.
counterexample.verified_how: Constructed deliberately via a targeted, non-random method (decomposing games into 'pieces' terminated by jacks, a template-based search for pieces, and backward-play reconstruction), then verified by direct simulation of the resulting deal; the construction and periodicity proof were later checked by peer review for the American Mathematical Monthly.

summary: The question 'Is there a non-terminating game of Beggar-My-Neighbour?' (Wikipedia's January 2024 wording of a problem John Conway called an 'anti-Hilbert problem') was answered affirmatively shortly after the frozen revision's date. Brayden Casella found a concrete non-terminating starting configuration on 10 February 2024 (per Richard P. Mann's Beggar-My-Neighbour records page and the Wikipedia article's current text), and Casella together with seven collaborators (Anderson, Kleber, Mann, Nessler, Rucklidge, Williams, Wu) wrote up the construction and proof, posting it to arXiv on 19 March 2024 (arXiv:2403.13855, 'A Non-Terminating Game of Beggar-My-Neighbor'). This was subsequently peer-reviewed and published in The American Mathematical Monthly, vol. 132, no. 10 (2025), pp. 978-994, on 20 October 2025 — a formal expert digestion via peer review, so status is 'resolved' rather than merely 'claimed'. The method was entirely classical: the authors describe decomposing games into independent 'pieces' bounded by jacks, a template-based search over candidate pieces ('any sequence can replace TEST in this template... if the game is non-terminating with this sequence, then the sequence is a piece and can be saved'), and reasoning about backward (non-deterministic) play to stitch pieces into a full cyclical game — plus earlier statistical/brute-force random search attempts that failed before the targeted construction succeeded. No machine learning, neural network, or AI system of any kind is mentioned anywhere in the paper, in Olly Britton's detailed blog write-up of the discovery process, or in the Wikipedia article. A 2026 follow-up preprint (arXiv:2602.23406, 'The Dynamical Landscape of Beggar-My-Neighbour: Ultra-long Matches, Loops, and Infinite Matches', posted 24 August 2026, by Andorno, Cernoia, Duiz, and Michelangeli) builds on the 2024 result with a heuristic 'Infinite Loop Factory' algorithm using backward dynamics reconstruction and 'adaptive insertion strategies' to systematize the discovery of further non-terminating cycles — again explicitly a heuristic/algorithmic search, not AI/ML, and it does not re-resolve the existence question, which was already settled in 2024; it is mentioned here for completeness but does not change the classification.
competing_reading: One could argue for 'claimed' rather than 'resolved' if one requires the specific Monthly peer review to be the only acceptable digestion and discounts the fact that the result circulated and was informally checked (e.g., via community verification and Wikipedia's own updated article) for over a year before formal publication; but since the paper has in fact been peer-reviewed and published in a journal of record (American Mathematical Monthly), 'resolved' is the correct code per §6.1.
what_would_settle_it: The published Monthly article version already settles the classification; no further evidence is needed. (Only genuinely open would be independent replication of the specific card sequence, which is trivial to check by simulation and has been done by the community, e.g. via the referenced BeggarMyPython utility.)
